scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

First, the girlfriend has been asking the guy to handle car issues, like checking tire pressure and pumping air. He initially helped, even bought a PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. But now she's asking him to do it every morning and take her to the gas station. He's frustrated because she's not learning, and she's relying on strangers (men) to do tasks he taught her. He's also upset that she's acting helpless and that her male friends agree with her about it being a man's responsibility. He's tired of the gender roles and doesn't want to be seen as a "man" just because he does certain things. He's decided not to help anymore, and the question is whether that's morally acceptable.

So, the key points here are about responsibility, gender roles, and mutual respect in a relationship. The guy is trying to set boundaries, not wanting to be forced into a role that's based on outdated stereotypes. He's also doing a lot around the house and paying expenses, so he's not the one in need of help. The girlfriend is expecting him to do tasks he's already taught her, but she's not taking initiative. He's pointing out that she's playing the "damsel in distress" role, which he finds problematic.

From a moral standpoint, the action of refusing to help might be seen as standing up for personal boundaries. He's not being unhelpful; he's asserting that he doesn't want to be in a position where he's expected to do things based on gender stereotypes. However, the girlfriend is relying on him for tasks that she's capable of doing, which he's already taught her. There's a power dynamic here where she's expecting him to take on responsibilities that are not his to bear, and he's trying to correct that.

But is refusing to help morally acceptable? It depends on whether the refusal is based on a fair assessment of the situation. He's not refusing out of selfishness, but because he's tired of the gender roles and the lack of mutual effort. The girlfriend is not taking the initiative to learn and apply the skills he's given her. He's trying to encourage her to be independent and not rely on him for things she can do herself. So, his refusal might be a way to push her to take responsibility, which could be seen as morally acceptable because it's about promoting self-reliance and mutual respect.

However, there's also the aspect of the girlfriend's safety. If she's relying on strangers to help, there might be a risk, especially if she's in an unsafe area. But the user mentioned that he's already shown her how to do it, so the responsibility should be on her to use that knowledge. The guy's refusal is about not being forced into a role that's not fair, and he's not the one who's in the wrong here. He's trying to correct a situation where he's being treated as the default problem-solver, which is a gender stereotype.

In terms of morality, it's about fairness and respect. If the girlfriend is not taking the initiative and the guy is trying to set boundaries, then his refusal could be seen as morally acceptable because he's not being coercive. He's not refusing to help out of malice, but because he's trying to maintain his own boundaries and encourage her to be independent. So, the answer would be 1, morally acceptable.
